label: Deponent verbs
blurb: Verbs that look passive but mean active, especially their imperatives in -re (singular) and -minī (plural).
what_to_mark: Deponent imperatives: singular in -re (sequere, opperīre, revertere, oblīvīscere, proficīscere) and plural in -minī (laetāminī, intuēminī, sequiminī).
Deponent finite forms in every tense: present and future (polliceor, pollicentur, loquor, revertar), perfect (profectus est, secūta est, oblīta sum), pluperfect (pollicitus erat, oblītus erat).
Deponent infinitives in -ī / -rī (loquī, oblīvīscī).
Deponent perfect participles with active meaning (locūta, secūtus, arbitrātus).
Do not mark true passives of ordinary verbs (mittēbantur, vorābantur, necātus est) or the passive-of-faciō fīō (factus est); the note may contrast them.
Optional preview: ad + gerund purpose phrases (ad nāvigandum, ad fugiendum) labelled 'gerund of purpose (preview)'.

label: Gerund
blurb: The verb used as a noun: ad + -ndum for purpose, -ndī with a noun or causā, -ndō for means.
what_to_mark: ad + gerund expressing purpose (ad nāvigandum, ad volandum).
Genitive gerund in -ndī after a noun or adjective (ars volandī, cupidus discendī) and with causā/grātiā.
Ablative gerund in -ndō for means or with in/dē/ab (volandō, in scrībendō).
Gerund with an object (ad ālās faciendum) — note in the tag that Ørberg keeps the gerund + accusative rather than the gerundive here.
Do not mark gerundives (adjective-shaped -ndus/-nda, agreeing with a noun); they are Week 9. Do not mark secundum, nondum, or the noun-forms in -ndum that are not verbal.

label: Present subjunctive and supine
blurb: Indirect commands with ut/nē + present subjunctive, plus the supine in -um (after motion) and -ū (with adjectives).
what_to_mark: Present subjunctive in ut/nē clauses after verbs of asking, ordering, persuading (imperat ut veniat; ōrat nē discēdat).
Present subjunctive in purpose clauses (ut videat) and after verbs of fearing (timet nē).
Hortatory/jussive present subjunctive in main clauses (eāmus, nē timeat).
Supine in -um after a verb of motion to express purpose (dormītum it, spectātum vēnērunt).
Supine in -ū with an adjective (mīrābile dictū, facile factū).
Distinguish future indicative of 3rd/4th conjugation (-et/-ent, -iet) from present subjunctive of 1st conjugation (-et/-ent): mark only the subjunctives; the note can point out the look-alike.

label: Present subjunctive
blurb: Present subjunctive across all conjugations, in ut/nē clauses of purpose and indirect command and in main-clause wishes and exhortations.
what_to_mark: Every present subjunctive verb form, active and passive, including irregulars (sim, possim, velim, eam, feram).
The ut/nē that introduces it, in the same highlight when adjacent, so the learner sees the pair (ut … veniat).
Indirect command after imperō, ōrō, rogō, moneō, hortor, persuādeō, cūrō, cavē (nē).
Purpose clauses (ut … videat), including relative purpose (quī … faciat).
Main-clause subjunctives: hortatory (eāmus), jussive (veniat), prohibitive with nē.
Note in the tag how the tense of the main verb is present/future (primary sequence) — this sets up Weeks 5–6.

label: Imperfect subjunctive
blurb: Imperfect subjunctive (infinitive + endings) after a past main verb: result, purpose, indirect command, indirect question.
what_to_mark: Every imperfect subjunctive form, active (-rem, -rēs, -ret, -rēmus, -rētis, -rent: the infinitive plus endings) and passive (-rer, -rēris, -rētur, -rēmur, -rēminī, -rentur), including essem, possem, vellem, īrem, ferrem.
Result clauses signalled by tam, tantus, ita, sīc, adeō, tot, tālis + ut … (nōn).
Purpose clauses ut/nē + imperfect subjunctive after a past main verb.
Indirect commands after past verbs of asking or ordering (imperāvit ut … mitterent).
Indirect questions introduced by quis, quid, cūr, quōmodo, ubi, unde, num, utrum … an, after verbs of asking, knowing, telling.
In each note name the introducing word and the past main verb that makes the tense imperfect (function before form).

label: Imperfect subjunctive and sequence of tenses
blurb: Imperfect subjunctive again, now watching the main verb: present/future main verb takes present subjunctive, past main verb takes imperfect.
what_to_mark: Every imperfect subjunctive form (see Week 5 patterns) and every present subjunctive in the same passage, labelled so the learner can compare them.
The main verb that governs each subordinate subjunctive; mention its tense in the note ('rogābat (past) so the clause takes imperfect subjunctive').
Indirect questions after past verbs (nesciēbat ubi esset), and any indirect question with present subjunctive after a present verb (nesciō ubi sit) for contrast.
Purpose and indirect command after past verbs (vēnit ut … vidēret; imperāvit nē … abīrent).
cum + imperfect subjunctive ('when/since', circumstantial) if it appears, labelled as a preview of Week 7.

label: ut/nē clauses, deliberative subjunctive, cum clauses
blurb: Telling apart indirect command, purpose and result after ut/nē; questions of 'what am I to do?'; cum with the subjunctive.
what_to_mark: Every ut/nē clause, labelled by function: indirect command (after verbs of ordering/asking), purpose ('in order to'), result (after tam/ita/tantus, negative ut nōn), fearing (timeō nē).
Deliberative subjunctive in a question, usually first person (quid faciam? quō eāmus?), including negative quid nōn faciam.
cum + subjunctive: circumstantial ('when'), causal ('since'), concessive ('although', often with tamen). Distinguish from cum + ablative ('with') and cum + indicative for a definite time.
Subjunctive after nē alone in prohibitions or after verbs of fearing; ut nōn in result clauses.
In the note, name the test the learner can apply: is there an ordering verb (command)? a 'so … that' word (result)? could you add 'in order' (purpose)?

label: Future perfect
blurb: The future perfect in sī/cum/antequam/postquam/ubi clauses: 'when you (will) have done X, Y will happen'.
what_to_mark: Every future perfect form: active -erō, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint (perfect stem) and passive perfect participle + erō/eris/erit.
The conjunction that introduces it: sī, nisi, cum, antequam, priusquam, ubi, postquam, simul atque, dum.
The future main verb it pairs with, so the note can say 'the sail will be changed (future) once the Minotaur has been killed (future perfect)'.

Watch look-alikes: -eris/-erit/-erint are also perfect subjunctive (Week 10); -erō/-erimus are unambiguous. Mark by sense (indicative in a time/condition clause) and mention the ambiguity in the note where the form is shared.
Also mark fuerō/fuerit and potuerō/potuerit, and voluerit, ierit if present.

label: Gerundive and passive periphrastic
blurb: The -ndus adjective: with sum it says what must be done, and the person who must do it goes into the dative.
what_to_mark: Gerundive + form of sum (passive periphrastic): laudandus est, vīnum bibendum est, dormiendum est (impersonal). Include the sum form in the span when adjacent.
The dative of agent that goes with it (mihi, tibi, nōbīs, servīs, or a noun in -ō/-ī/-ibus), labelled 'dative of agent' with a note 'the person who must do it'.
Gerundive used attributively or after ad in place of ad + gerund + object (ad epistulam scrībendam, in place of ad epistulam scrībendum), agreeing with its noun.
Impersonal periphrastic with an intransitive verb (eundum est, pugnandum est).
Do not mark gerunds (Week 2) unless directly contrasted; -ndum with sum or agreeing with a noun is a gerundive.

label: Perfect subjunctive
blurb: Perfect subjunctive (-erim, -eris, -erit …): nē + perfect subjunctive for 'don't', and indirect questions about the past after a present verb.
what_to_mark: Every perfect subjunctive form: active -erim, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint; passive perfect participle + sim/sīs/sit/sīmus/sītis/sint; fuerim, potuerim.
Prohibitions nē + perfect subjunctive (nē timueris, nē dīxerītis), labelled 'prohibition' with a note comparing nōlī + infinitive.
Indirect questions about a past event after a present main verb (nesciō quid fēcerit; rogat cūr vēnerint), with the question word in the note.
Perfect subjunctive in primary-sequence result or consecutive clauses if any (rare).
Look-alikes: -eris/-erit/-erint also future perfect (Week 8). In a nē-prohibition or an indirect question it is subjunctive; in a sī/cum time clause with a future main verb it is future perfect.

label: Perfect subjunctive and wishes with utinam
blurb: More perfect subjunctive, plus utinam (nē) + subjunctive for wishes: present for the future, imperfect and pluperfect for wishes that cannot come true.
what_to_mark: Every perfect subjunctive form (see Week 10), in indirect questions and prohibitions.

utinam / utinam nē + subjunctive: present subjunctive for a wish still possible ('may he come'), imperfect for a present unreal wish ('if only he were here'), pluperfect for a past unreal wish ('if only he had come'). Label the tense and say in the note whether the wish can still come true.
Wishes without utinam if the subjunctive stands alone in a main clause with wish sense (dī tē servent, valeant).
The negative nē (not nōn) in a wish or prohibition.

label: Pluperfect subjunctive and future imperative
blurb: Pluperfect subjunctive (-issem …) in 'if X had happened, Y would have happened' and past wishes; the future imperative (estō, mementō) for standing orders.
what_to_mark: Every pluperfect subjunctive form: active -issem, -issēs, -isset, -issēmus, -issētis, -issent (perfect stem); passive perfect participle + essem/essēs/esset/essent; fuissem, potuissem.

Contrary-to-fact conditions: sī + pluperfect subjunctive in the if-clause, pluperfect (or imperfect) subjunctive in the main clause. Mark both halves; say in the note which part is the condition and that neither happened.
Imperfect subjunctive in present contrary-to-fact conditions (sī habērem, darem) for contrast.
Past wishes utinam + pluperfect subjunctive (utinam vēnisset).
cum + pluperfect subjunctive ('when he had …') in narrative.
Future imperative in -tō/-tōte/-ntō: estō, estōte, mementō, scītō, and any 2nd-person -tō forms in rules or laws; note that it gives an order for the future or a general rule.

label: Poetry: elegiac couplet and hendecasyllable; dummodo; dative verbs
blurb: First verse: the elegiac couplet (hexameter + pentameter) and the hendecasyllable; dummodo 'provided that' + subjunctive; verbs whose object is in the dative.
what_to_mark: Verse units: label each couplet or line by metre ('elegiac couplet: hexameter line', 'pentameter line', 'hendecasyllable') from the unit_type/verse position rather than a regex; the note names the poet (Ovid, Catullus, Martial) and the metre.
dummodo (and modo / dum in the sense 'provided that') + subjunctive, with the note 'a condition that must hold: provided that'.

Verbs that take a dative object: pāreō, placeō, displiceō, noceō, persuādeō, imperō, serviō, studeō, faveō, crēdō, ignōscō, invideō, resistō, and compounds of sum (adsum, dēsum, prōsum). Mark the verb and its dative in one span when adjacent; note 'the dative is the object here, where English uses a direct object'.
Poetic word order worth a note: adjective separated from its noun across the line, verb at the end, postponed conjunctions.
Ōdī et amō (Catullus 85) stays in Week 13; Week 14 starts at Hīs versibus recitātīs.

label: Poetry: prosody, elision, scansion; Martial
blurb: Reading verse aloud: long and short syllables, elision when a vowel or -m meets a following vowel, scanning the hexameter and pentameter; Martial's epigrams and their final point.
what_to_mark: Elision sites: a word ending in a vowel or -m followed by a word beginning with a vowel or h- (e.g. 'Ōdī et amō' becomes ōd(ī) et amō). Mark the two-word span; the note says which vowel drops.
Syllables long by position (vowel before two consonants) where a learner would guess short, and diphthongs; mark a word and explain the quantity in the note.
The caesura in the hexameter and the fixed second half of the pentameter, marked on the line unit with a note on where the pause falls.
Each Martial epigram's turn or point (the last line), labelled 'epigram: the point' with the joke explained in plain English.
Any remaining Week 13 constructions (dative verbs, dummodo) if they recur, using the Week 13 labels.
Scansion itself is not regex-able: the unit_type 'verse' and line position decide which units get metre labels.
